summary: Campaign 34's four hinted arms each submitted 31.6-31.9 M tokens of SSD writes: over the run 38-49 % were prompt pages later read back from the SSD (4.0-4.8 times each), 21-31 % were only ever served from memory, 15 % were output nodes the replay never re-sends, 3.9 % were a session's final request, and in ec_full's minutes 60-100 the read-back share is 57 %. R1 would have saved 1.47 M tokens (4.6 %, under 1 % of the device at saturation; 0.22-0.24 M if the end is only known at the reply), and an oracle that writes only what is later read back saves 46-58 % over the run, about 43 % at saturation (22 % without outputs and resubmits). Write due dates are real under forecast eviction: in ec_full at least 3.6 % of live sessions' prompt pages (estimate 14 %) were out of memory within 5 s of their write's ack and 16 % within 30 s (ec_exact 2.9 % and 13 %, LRU 0.0 % and 0.1 %), and the engine's own lines show 1,233 chains gone within 5 s of the commit; no page was seen out of memory before its ack in any arm, campaign 32's 57-59 s write lags included. A pending write holds its node's whole host-only chain, 4.6-6.9 times its own tokens in the census (p90 58-92 K, max 244-376 K against about 0.9 M of room), so pending tokens (p90 10-15 K) understate the dirty set. On the device a write op pays a fixed 150-200 ms whenever a read is in progress (4.6 ms alone for one page); merged writes run at 11 ms a page against 3.1 alone and reads at 3.5 against 2.4, and at saturation reads move 17.3-18.1 K and writes 3.4-4.3 K of the 21.4 K tokens/s. Fix 3's hold fired 27-30 times per arm, every time on the prompt write of a request still running (which holds nothing eviction could take), cost at most 9-15 s of read-thread time per run, and no eviction came back short; the draft's room rule would have fired 0 times at this setting and write order would change nothing there (writes are acked a median 0.6-0.8 s after submit). In campaign 32 the first refusals came when 49-105 small FIFO write ops, 8-17 s old and only 37-90 K tokens, sat on chains bounded at 0.64-1.2 M tokens (about 0.77 of that held, by campaign 34's calibration), which is most of the host-only memory and accounts for the room that record could not attribute; by an estimated room the draft's rule turns true 1-53 s before all 12 bursts and the 50 K rule 14-57 s before 11 of them (inferred). By the first cleaner pass 76 % of the SSD's 22.5 M tokens belonged to ended sessions (17.0 M against 4.4 M of prompt pages of sessions in progress), so every pass (2.5-2.7 M) could have come from ended sessions alone; today's oldest-first pass took only 0.04-0.10 M tokens from sessions in progress, yet that cost 1.05-1.19 M tokens of recompute per arm, plus 0.23-0.24 M through shared heads that a tails-before-heads order would have kept. Not established: exact eviction times (no log line names an evicted node, so slack is bracketed), any TTFT effect, R3 (no write failed in these runs), and whether a hold or a write order would in fact have stopped campaign 32's refusals (needs a GPU run).

findings.question: 1a. What did the SSD writes buy? Split of submitted tokens by class, device time, and when in the run (campaign 34).
findings.answer: Submitted: 31.60 M tokens in 33,973 ops (ec_full), 31.82 M (jit_exact), 31.87 M (jit_p50), 31.65 M (ec_exact). Share of submitted tokens, ec_full / jit_exact / jit_p50 / ec_exact: prompt pages of non-final turns read back from the SSD at least once 42.3 / 38.3 / 49.0 / 40.5 % (13.4 / 12.2 / 15.6 / 12.8 M, each read 4.5 / 4.0 / 4.8 / 4.0 times; 86-87 % of those reads by the session that wrote the page, 13-14 % by another session sharing the prefix); never read back, later requests got them from GPU or host memory every time 27.3 / 30.8 / 21.2 / 29.5 %; never read back and no later request held the page 5.5 / 4.9 / 3.2 / 5.0 % (ec_full: 1.36 M dropped by the next prompt, 0.38 M cut off by the run's end); needed again but computed again 0.8 / 1.1 / 1.0 / 0.9 %; prompt pages of a session's final request 3.9 % in every arm (1.24 M); output nodes 15.2 / 15.0 / 15.0 / 15.2 % (4.78-4.81 M, the replay artifact; 0.22-0.24 M of it from final requests); keys submitted a second time 4.9 / 5.9 / 6.7 / 4.8 % (fix 1 skipped 1.07-1.71 M tokens as stored); not joined 0.03-0.15 %. Of live sessions' prompt pages alone 55.8 / 51.0 / 65.9 / 53.4 % were read back. By submit time in ec_full: read back 28 % (minutes 0-30), 41 % (30-60), 57 % (60-90) and 55-59 % in each 10 minutes from 60 to 100; memory-only 49 / 33 / 13 %. Write thread busy 3,066-4,026 s per run (3,341 s in ec_full); output nodes take 28-32 % of it for 15 % of the tokens (15.6 K small ops). Staged (pre-arrival) reads pulled 0.49 M tokens of dead output nodes in jit_p50 (of 34.1 M staged), 0.05 M in jit_exact, 0.03 M in ec_exact. hicache: 94.74 M submitted, 78.5 % second submits (79 % of pages skipped as stored), 6.0 % read back. Campaign 32 ec_full for contrast: 45.43 M submitted, 34 % second submits over the run and 64 % in minutes 90-120 (10 % not joined).
findings.method: scripts/q1_writes.py on a page-level model (scripts/model.py, pages.py, lib.py). Each h2s_submit op is tied to its request through the scheduler step that produced it: the step's ReqTimeStats or Prefill batch line, then d2h_submit; copies are acked in order and an ack's h2s_submit lines sit just before its d2h_done line (all 27,473 transfers of ec_full sum exactly, out/fifo_check.out). Prompt pages get the key (scope, id of the page's last 16-token block) from the trace, which is equal across sessions exactly when the engine's chained page hash is. Every s2h_io is placed on its chain from the prefetch_start before it (2,675 of 2,678 reads in ec_full). Join: 99.85-99.97 % of submitted tokens in the hinted arms, 99.4 % in hicache, about 90 % in campaign 32 (out/model_build_c34.out, model_build_c32.out, join_check_c34.out). Outputs: out/q1_c34_<arm>.out, q1_c34_<arm>_10min.out, q1_who_reads_c34.out, q1_c34.json.
findings.implication: Eager writing is right for live sessions once the box is saturated: 57-59 % of submitted tokens, about three quarters of live prompt pages, are read back, 4-5 times each. What is wasted there is small and spread over five classes. The replay artifact is 15 % of write tokens but 28-32 % of the write thread's time, so write-path numbers are that much pessimistic against a harness that re-sends outputs. Pages written in the last 20 minutes are censored by the run's end, so their read-back shares are lower bounds.

findings.question: 1b. How many tokens would R1 (skip an ended session's last write) have saved, and what does it need?
findings.answer: 1.47-1.48 M tokens per arm (4.6-4.7 % of submitted; 130-177 s = 4.2-4.4 % of the write thread's time): 1.24 M of prompt pages plus 0.22-0.24 M of output nodes of the 566-571 sessions that ended. Only the 0.22-0.24 M (0.7-0.8 %) if the end is known at the reply and not when the prompt is inserted. Of the skipped pages 0.016-0.026 M were later read back by another session. At saturation (minutes 90-110, writes 3.4-4.3 K of 21.4 K tokens/s) it is about 0.1-0.2 K tokens/s, under 1 % of the device. The engine's present end signal cannot drive it: in the two table-hint arms 411 commits per run were registered ended that were not the session's last request (no table entry for the reply key: next_turn_prefetch.py:609 returns None and :521 registers the end), and those turns' writes were 2.27 M tokens of which 1.78 M (ec_full) and 1.55 M (jit_p50) were later read back. The exact-hint arms have 56-57 such commits, all sessions the run's end cut.
findings.method: scripts/q1_writes.py; a session ended when the trace stream's last request was sent; the engine's view is the nue_register line next to each request's ReqTimeStats line (next_use_ms=ended). out/q1_c34_<arm>.out (lines 'R1', 'engine's end signal', 'engine_said_ended_but_live_*').
findings.implication: As a device saving R1 is not worth building on its own: under 1 % of device time and a first cleaner pass about 4 minutes later. If built, key it on the explicit end entry, never on 'no hint'. The prompt part needs the end before the reply; a way round (inferred, untested) is to submit a turn's writes at its commit, since a running request's pages are GPU-locked mirror that eviction cannot take, which would also halve write transfers (2 per request today). R1's real value is its second half, the SSD order (finding 4).

findings.question: 1c. How much would an oracle that writes only what is evicted before its next use have saved?
findings.answer: It needs 14.52 / 13.53 / 17.30 / 13.89 M tokens (ec_full / jit_exact / jit_p50 / ec_exact) and saves 54.1 / 57.5 / 45.7 / 56.1 % of submitted tokens (53.3 / 56.4 / 44.7 / 55.3 % if pages that had to be computed again count as needed). The saving is front-loaded. In ec_full's minutes 60-100 it is 43 %: output nodes 15.5 %, memory-only 11.6 %, no later use 5.6 %, second submits 5.5 % (fix 1 already skips them), final requests 3.4 %, lost 1.5 %; about 22 % once outputs and second submits are set aside. In minutes 90-110 that is about 1.2-1.6 K of the device's 21.4 K tokens/s (6-7 %). It would also halve the SSD's fill rate: the 22.6 M-token mark that starts the cleaner at minute 88 would not be reached in 2 h.
findings.method: scripts/q1_writes.py: a write is needed when an SSD read of its page starts after it and before the next submit of the same key. Windows from out/q1_c34_w600.json and q1_c34_ec_full_10min.out; device shares from out/q3_c34_ec_full.out part E. The device and fill-rate conversions are arithmetic on those numbers.
findings.implication: Deferring writes to their due date (section 4.2) buys at most a 6-7 % larger read share at saturation and nothing at light load, where the device is idle. Through device time it does not pay at this setting; its measurable value is SSD capacity (fewer cleaner passes).

findings.question: 2. Due dates: when did each written page's host copy go, how long before that was its write done, and did any page leave before its write finished?
findings.answer: Write submit to ack per page: p50 0.59-0.77 s, p90 1.80-2.23 s, p99 3.45-4.24 s, max 5.69-6.91 s (hinted arms). Pages seen out of memory before their ack: 0 in all five campaign 34 arms and 0 in campaign 32 ec_full and jit_exact, where the lag is p90 31 s and max 57-59 s. Share of live sessions' prompt pages (24.0 M tokens in ec_full) seen out of memory less than 5 s after the ack, at least: ec_full 3.57 %, ec_exact 2.87 %, jit_p50 1.43 %, jit_exact 0.46 %, hicache 0.00 %; less than 30 s: 16.4 / 12.9 / 14.5 / 5.1 / 0.13 %. Upper bounds (last seen in memory less than 5 s after the ack): 28.0 / 21.6 / 29.2 / 23.0 / 21.4 %. Estimate (interval-censored NPMLE) of slack <= 5 s: 14.2 / 10.0 / 8.2 / 2.8 / 0.0 %; <= 30 s: 23.7 / 17.3 / 24.2 / 9.7 / 0.5 %; <= 0.5 s: 3.5 / 2.6 / 0.4 / 0.1 / 0.0 %. Never seen missing: 32-47 %. In ec_full the tight ones precede human waits: 10-20 % of those pages within 5 s and 35-52 % within 30 s, against 1.3 % and 9.2 % before a tool call that returned in under 5 s. Join-free check on the engine's own ec_start lines: from minute 30, 1,233 of ec_full's 1,905 chains that lost 256 tokens or more before the next turn were first seen so within 5 s of the commit (191 within 1 s; median 25-28 K tokens missing; the whole chain in 926); ec_exact 1,242 of 1,723. Traced case (ec_full c152 t12): finish at 3,731.06 s, last write ack 3,732.063 s, host eviction of 46.7 K tokens at 3,732.112 s (49 ms later), whole 41,472-token chain missing at 3,732.59 s. Under LRU (hicache) 0 of 99,650 pages first observed under 10 s were missing, 15 of 66,032 at 10-30 s, 6.8 % at 30-60 s, 38 % at 60-120 s.
findings.method: scripts/q2_due.py, q2_by_gap.py, q2_before_done.py, ec_start_idle.py. No log line names an evicted node (evict_host and evict_device carry token counts only), so each page's exit is bracketed: every prefetch_start gives the resident prefix (GPU plus host) of its key, ec_start and ntp_due case 1 give it for an idle session's chain, and a second submit of a key proves the page had left. Slack lies between (last seen in memory - ack) and (first seen missing - ack); 89-92 % of pages have an observation. For the next_use arms (jit_p50, jit_exact) nothing is logged during the idle gap, so their lower bounds are weak. Outputs: out/q2_c34_<arm>.out, q2_by_gap_c34.out, ec_start_idle.out, q2_c32_<arm>.out.
findings.implication: The draft's due date d_w exists, and under an index policy at saturation it is 'at the commit' for the sessions the index ranks lowest: for about a tenth of turns the eager write is already just in time, so there is no slack to defer into and nothing for a due-date order to gain while writes take 0.6-0.8 s. Under LRU no write is within 30 s of its due date. 'Not worth writing yet' is usable only for sessions the index ranks high. The lock on dirty pages holds (0 violations), so R3's remaining case is a failed write, and none occurred in these runs (0 failed groups, no 'pages failed' line): R3 has no test here.

findings.question: 2b. How large was the dirty set against free plus evictable clean room?
findings.answer: Census lines from minute 30 (534-538 per arm): pending write tokens median 0-1 K, p90 10-15 K, max 52-68 K. Tokens that only pending writes hold (h_write: the written node plus every host-only ancestor, since host eviction takes leaves only) median 0, p90 58-92 K (0 in hicache), max 244-376 K. Free + evictable room (free + evict_leaf + evict_casc) p10 456-915 K, median 648-980 K. Ratios: pending/room p90 0.011-0.026, max 0.06-0.17; held-by-writes/room p90 0.07-0.17, max 0.40-1.01; held-by-writes/host-only p90 6-10 %, max 27-42 %. Summed over the lines, writes hold 4.6-6.9 times their own pending tokens. At each submit pending is p50 0.5-2.6 K, p99 40-49 K, max 59-87 K; 0.2-1.0 % of submits see 50 K or more.
findings.method: scripts/census_dirty.py and the census part of q2_due.py on the host_census lines; scripts/write_held.py calibrate compares the census with a bound built from the join (chains of sessions whose finished request has a pending write): the bound is at or above the census's h_write on 2,151 of 2,152 lines and held/bound is 0.74-0.79. Outputs: out/census_dirty_c34.out, write_held_calibrate_c34.out.
findings.implication: Section 1.2's 'dirty page' must be a dirty chain: a late write costs lambda x (the leaf + its host-only ancestors), 5-7 times L_p here, and every room rule (5.1, 5.2, P2) should count tokens held by writes, not pending tokens. At campaign 34's setting the dirty set never bound room: no eviction came back short of what was asked before the deadline.

findings.question: 3a. When did writes delay reads and reads delay writes on the device?
findings.answer: Reads delay writes by a fixed wait per write op: unmerged ops alone against with a read in progress (campaign 34 ec_full; campaign 32 ec_full in brackets): 1 page 4.5 ms against 175 ms (149), 2-4 pages 10 against 198 (155), 5-16 pages 28 against 221 (184), 17-64 pages 90 against 326 (293), 65-128 pages 357 against 571 (796). Over all writes: 3.06-3.13 ms a page alone, 10.9-11.8 with a read. Writes delay reads by about their own length: reads 2.41-2.69 ms a page alone, 3.53-3.73 when a write overlaps half or more of the read. iostat at 95 % util or more: 2,004-2,009 MiB/s in every arm = 21.4 K tokens/s. When: ec_full's read thread is 39 % busy in minutes 60-70, 74 % in 70-80, 86 % in 80-90, 99.6-99.9 % in 90-110 (jit_p50 99.9 % from minute 70); the write thread goes from 40 to 74 % busy; submit-to-ack p50 0.03-0.05 s (minutes 0-30), 0.10-0.14 (30-60), 0.45-0.58 (70-110), p90 at most 1.65 s; timed reads parked p50 13-15 s (70-90) and 41-43 s (90-110). At saturation reads move 17.3-18.1 K and writes 3.4-4.3 K tokens/s. Campaign 32 without merging: write lag p50/p90 0.32/1.8 s (60-70), 3.6/12.9 s (70-80), 10.9/40 s (80-90), 39/52 s (90-100), reads and writes ending at 10.6 and 10.7 K tokens/s.
findings.method: scripts/q3_rw.py parts D and E and scripts/op_cost.py: read busy intervals from s2h_io (end minus ms), write busy from h2s_io and h2s_group; campaign34/iostat_vdc.log by run window. The cause of the fixed wait (a write transfer waiting for the read's current batch on the one NIXL agent, storage/nixl/hicache_nixl.py:121-131) is inferred from the timing, not read in NIXL. Outputs: out/q3_c34_<arm>.out, q3_c32_<arm>.out, op_cost.out.
findings.implication: The device model of sections 1.2 and 5.2 needs a per-transfer term: under a busy read thread a write costs 0.15-0.2 s per transfer, not L/beta, so write capacity is 5-6 transfers a second against about 4.7 arriving unmerged. Merging (fix 2) is what keeps the dirty set bounded, and stability claim 7.9 should be stated in transfers. Reads against writes can be ordered at the grain of a 128-page batch.

findings.question: 3b. What did fix 3's hold cost readers, what did it protect, and would the draft's rule or writes in eviction order change anything at campaign 34's setting?
findings.answer: Holds before the deadline: 30 / 27 / 30 / 29 (ec_full / jit_exact / jit_p50 / ec_exact), 57-81 s in all per arm, median 1.9-2.8 s, max 3.9-8.2 s. Cost: 240-491 timed reads (6.1-12.9 M tokens) were parked across a hold; their parked time inside holds is 558-1,676 s, 1.0-1.4 % of all timed-read parking (52.8-119 K s); 4-13 were dispatched within 0.1 s of a hold's end; the read thread idled 9.3-14.5 s inside holds that had timed reads parked, at most 0.16-0.25 M tokens of reads put off (27-89 reader-seconds as idle time x reads parked). Protection: none measurable. At every hold but one (28 of 29 in ec_exact), over 80 % of the pending tokens (median 100 % of a median 53-56 K) were prompt nodes of a request still running, whose host copies are GPU mirror that eviction cannot take anyway; chains of finished requests under pending writes at the hold's start: median 0, p90 62-137 K, max 132-242 K. No eviction came back short in the run (0 of 5,498-6,181; jit_exact's 2 are at 7,221 s, after the deadline, with 846 K tokens of reads in flight). Draft's rule: free + evictable room over the allocation expected while the writes drain is at least 1.7-2.8 at the holds (median 3.7-14.9) and at least 2.1-4.2 on the 711-712 census lines per arm, so it would hold 0 times. Write order: writes hold a mean 18-30 K tokens (2-3 % of host-only memory) for a median 0.6-0.8 s.
findings.method: scripts/q3_rw.py parts A to C (srs_write_hold, srs_park, srs_dispatch, s2h_io, the census line before each hold, d2h_submit and read launches for the allocation rate, the write thread's tokens per busy second for the drain time) and scripts/holds_what.py (whose writes were pending at each hold's start). Outputs: out/q3_c34_<arm>.out, holds_what_c34.out, q3_c34.json.
findings.implication: At this setting P2 and R2 are worth nothing in TTFT: removing the 27-30 holds returns 9-15 s of read-thread time per 2 h run, and no write is late enough for its order to matter (that part is inferred from the measured bounds). The 50 K threshold measures the wrong thing: it counts tokens of running requests that hold no evictable memory. P2 should compare tokens held only by writes (the census's h_write) with the shortfall of free + evictable room, and hold only if draining writes would release it; when pins hold the room instead, the answer is Preempt, not a write hold.

findings.question: 3c. In campaign 32 (no fixes, no census) would the draft's rule or writes in eviction order have avoided the first refusals?
findings.answer: First refusals: ec_full at 4,617 s, jit_exact 4,603 s, jit_p50 1,942 s; 12 bursts in the three arms before or at the sustained loop. At each burst's start the write queue held 49-105 ops (82, 74, 105; 93, 76; 49, 58, 102), the oldest 8-17 s old, only 37-89 K tokens, nearly all small (64-1,472 tokens, each taking 50-460 ms). The chains of the 26-46 sessions whose finished request had a pending write total 0.64-1.2 M tokens; x 0.77 by campaign 34's calibration that is 0.5-0.9 M of at most 0.98 M host-only tokens. Pins were 0-58 K in ec_full and jit_exact (89-301 K in jit_p50), reads in flight 8-63 K, anchors of parked reads 0-145 K. The short evictions asked a median 15-34 K and freed a median 0-1 K; the refused reads were mostly timed (33 of 40, 53 of 55, 27 of 31). Same load, minutes 60 to 76.5, campaign 32 against 34 (ec_full): pending ops p90 28 against 6, oldest age p90 6.2 s against 0.8 s, pending tokens p90 26 K against 13 K, chains under pending writes p90 376 K against 70 K (max 839 K against 303 K). With an estimated room the draft's rule turns true 1-53 s before all 12 bursts (12 s or more before 10) and the 50 K rule 14-57 s before 11 of 12 (never in the minute before jit_p50's first); away from bursts the draft's rule would hold in 0.1 / 0.4 / 14.2 % of seconds (ec_full / jit_exact / jit_p50), the 50 K rule in 0.7 / 0.6 / 10.6 %. With reads held, the pending ops would run at 5-30 ms each, not 150-200 ms, so the queue drains in 1-3 s. A write order by room released per device-second would serve the chain the evictor asks for within one op (0.15-0.2 s), where FIFO takes 8-17 s.
findings.method: scripts/write_held.py first, c32_queue_at.py, c32_refused_kind.py, queue_compare.py, c32_rule.py on campaign 32's logs (refusals are srs_dispatch launched=0; short evictions are evict_host tokens < requested). The room estimate is 900 K (campaign 34's median) - 0.77 x chains under pending writes - parked anchors - reads in flight - pins; expected allocation is the last 30 s' rate x the age of the oldest pending write. Campaign 32's join covers about 90 % of write tokens. Outputs: out/write_held_first_c32.out, c32_queue_at_ec_full_4607.out, c32_refused_kind.out, queue_compare_60_76.out, c32_rule.out.
findings.implication: Campaign 32's first refusals were a write-latency event, not a write-volume one: small FIFO ops slowed by reads pinned whole chains. This confirms and sizes that record's guess (host-only ancestors of locked nodes) for the room no logged lock explained. Either hold rule would probably have fired in time, and so would an eviction-ordered write queue, but what removed the condition in campaign 34 is merging (fix 2). P2 and R2 are stability levers of campaign 32-to-34 size (5.8-9.5 s there, shared with fixes 1 and 2), not steady-state gains; a GPU run with fix 2 off and each rule alone is needed to show it.

findings.question: 4. How much of the SSD did ended sessions hold over time, and what would an ended-sessions-first cleaner have left of live sessions' pages at each logged pass?
findings.answer: Ended sessions' share of the store (prompt pages plus outputs) in ec_full: 42 % at minute 10, 59 % at 30, 72 % at 60, 76 % at 80. At pass 1 (5,263 s, 22.55 M tokens): ended sessions 14.25 M of prompt pages + 2.79 M of outputs (75.6 %), ended sessions' heads that a later session uses 0.35 M, sessions in progress 4.44 M of prompt pages (3.63 M needed again, 0.81 M dropped) + 0.72 M of outputs. Passes 2-4: 75-80 % ended. The other three arms are within 0.1 M of this. Each pass deletes 2.52-2.70 M tokens (39,400-42,200 pages); the ended pool is 16.7-18.0 M, 6-7 times a pass, so an ended-first cleaner takes 0 pages of sessions in progress at every logged pass. Today's oldest-first pass took 0.04-0.10 M tokens of sessions in progress (0.00-0.10 M needed again) and 0.00-0.12 M of ended sessions' shared heads; the youngest page deleted was written 74-79 minutes earlier. What that cost per arm: 39-45 requests computed 1.05-1.19 M tokens again because their first uncached page had been deleted while their session was in progress, and 40-43 requests 0.23-0.24 M because an ended session's shared head was gone. With tails before heads inside ended sessions, 0.000 M of shared heads go (0.03-0.14 M with oldest-first inside ended).
findings.method: scripts/q4_ssd.py: a page is stored from its write's ack, a second submit or fix 1's touch moves its file time, and each logged pass deletes the N oldest pages present when its scan started. Checks: the replayed store holds 351.4-354.0 K pages at the passes where the log says 90.0-90.7 % full; every lookup's first missing page is a page never written, one a replayed pass deleted (114-179 per arm) or unexplained (0-2 per arm). Each alternative order is evaluated against the store as it was at that pass, not replayed pass after pass. Outputs: out/q4_c34_<arm>.out, q4_c34.json.
findings.implication: R4 is worth building and R1's 'chain first out' half is where its value is: ended-first removes 82-84 % of the cleaner's recompute (1.05-1.19 of 1.3-1.4 M tokens per arm in the 22 minutes after the first pass) and tails-before-heads the rest. It needs a map from stored pages to sessions that still use them (a session in progress that reads a head from memory never refreshes its file time). At this load live sessions need about 5.2 M of the 22.5 M tokens, so the volume could be about 4 times smaller before a live page must go (the trajectory claim is inferred from pool sizes).

surprises: Under return-chance eviction a session's whole chain can leave GPU and host memory within a second or two of its turn's commit: 1,233 of ec_full's chains from minute 30 lost 256 tokens or more within 5 s of the commit (191 within 1 s), and in one traced case the host eviction of 46.7 K tokens came 49 ms after the last write ack. Under LRU nothing leaves within 30 s of its write.

A pending write holds 4.6-6.9 times its own tokens, because a dirty leaf pins every host-only ancestor. In campaign 32's first refusals 37-89 K pending tokens sat on chains bounded at 0.64-1.2 M: this is the room that record said no logged lock explained.

Fix 3's 50 K hold fired 27-30 times per arm in campaign 34 and every time on the cold prompt of a request still running, which holds nothing eviction could take. It protected nothing there; what kept campaign 32's condition away was merging.

A one-page write takes 4.6 ms alone and 150-180 ms when a read is in progress, and the wait is about the same up to 16 pages: the write side's unit of cost is the transfer, not the token.
